title: BVA Decision 25000010: 1. Entitlement to an increased disability rating of 20 percent, but no higher, for left knee instability effective May 3, 2011, is granted
text:
Citation Nr: 25000010
Decision Date: 01/02/25	Archive Date: 01/02/25

DOCKET NO. 15-00 118A
DATE: January 2, 2025

ORDER

1. Entitlement to an increased disability rating of 20 percent, but no higher, for left knee instability effective May 3, 2011, is granted. 

2. Entitlement to an increased disability rating of 30 percent, but no higher, for left knee instability from February 10, 2020, to April [Redacted], 2021, is granted.

3. Entitlement to an increased disability rating in excess of 10 percent for left knee strain prior to April 29, 2018, is denied. 

4. Entitlement to an increased disability rating in excess of 20 percent from left knee strain from April 29, 2018, to April [Redacted], 2021, is denied.  

5. Entitlement to a total disability rating based on individual unemployability (TDIU) due to service-connected disabilities prior to January 22, 2019, is denied. 

FINDINGS OF FACT

1. The overall evidentiary record shows that the severity of the Veteran's left knee instability was moderate throughout the period on appeal until February 10, 2020; after February 10, 2020, the Veteran's left knee instability was severe. 

2. The overall evidentiary record shows that the severity of the Veteran's left knee strain most closely approximated the criteria for a 10 percent disability evaluation prior to April 29, 2018, and most closely approximated the criteria for a 20 percent disability evaluation from April 29, 2018, to April [Redacted], 2021.  

3. The most probative evidence of record indicates that the Veteran's service-connected disabilities did not preclude him from substantially gainful employment prior to January 22, 2019.

CONCLUSIONS OF LAW

1. The criteria for an increased rating for left knee instability have been met. 38 U.S.C. §§ 1155, 5107; 38 C.F.R. §§ 4.1-4.14, 4.21, 4.40, 4.45, 4.46, 4.59, 4.71a, Diagnostic Codes 5256-5262.

2. The criteria for an increased rating for left knee strain have not been met. 38 U.S.C. §§ 1155, 5107; 38 C.F.R. §§ 4.1-4.14, 4.21, 4.40, 4.45, 4.46, 4.59, 4.71a, Diagnostic Codes 5256-5262.

3. The criteria for TDIU have not been met. 38 U.S.C. §§ 1155, 5107; 38 C.F.R. §§ 3.340, 3.341, 4.16(a).

REASONS AND BASES FOR FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS

The Veteran served on active duty from November 1943 to May 1946 and from September 1947 to May 1948. The Veteran died on April [Redacted], 2021, and the Appellant is his surviving spouse. 

This case has a long a complex procedural history. These matters come to the Board of Veterans' Appeals (Board) from a May 2012 rating decision issued by the Agency of Original Jurisdiction (AOJ). Since the May 2012 decision, the issues on appeal have been returned by the Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims (CAVC) in July 2019 and September 2021 Joint Motions for Partial Remands (JMRs). The JMRs were followed by Board remands. 

In September 2023, the Board remanded these matters and directed the AOJ to get clarification on the retrospective medical opinions obtained pursuant to a June 2023 Board remand regarding the Veteran's left knee strain, left knee instability, and the impact of the Veteran's service-connected disabilities on his ability to work. Specifically, the September 2023 Board remand requested clarification on the functional impact of the Veteran's left knee disabilities from May 2011 to April 2021; to estimate the Veteran's left knee range of motion during the  staged rating periods of May 2011 to April 2021; and to assess the Veteran's left knee instability  as mild, moderate, or severe, including consideration of his muscle strength, and whether the instability and swelling affected his range of motion. That information was obtained in October 2023.

In July 2024, the Board again remanded these matters, noting that the October 2023 examination and opinion failed to adequately discuss and consider the entirety of the record. Specifically, the October 2023 examiner did not discuss the Veteran's lay statements or private medical records regarding the severity of his left knee disabilities and instead relied too heavily on prior VA examinations which had been determined to be inadequate in prior Board and CAVC decisions.

In August and October 2024, additional examination of the Veteran's record and medical opinion was provided by the examiner who provided the October 2023 examination and opinion. The Board finds that its remand instructions were substantially complied with. Stegall v. West, 11 Vet. App. 268 (1998).

Left Knee Strain and Left Knee Instability

Disability ratings are determined by applying the criteria set forth in the VA Schedule for Rating Disabilities, found in 38 C.F.R., Part 4. The ratings are intended to compensate, as far as can practicably be determined, the average impairment of earning capacity resulting from such diseases and injuries and their residual conditions in civilian occupations. 38 U.S.C. § 1155; 38 C.F.R. § 4.1. Where there is a question as to which of two evaluations shall be applied, the higher evaluation will be assigned if the disability picture more nearly approximates the criteria for that rating. 38 C.F.R. § 4.7.

When evaluating musculoskeletal disabilities based on limitation of motion, 38 C.F.R. § 4.40 requires consideration of functional loss caused by pain or other factors listed in that section that could occur during flare-ups or after repeated use and, therefore, not be reflected on range-of-motion testing. With respect to joints, in particular, the factors of disability reside in reductions of normal excursion of movements in different planes. 38 C.F.R. § 4.45 requires consideration also be given to less movement than normal, more movement than normal, weakened movement, excess fatigability, incoordination, and pain on movement. See DeLuca v. Brown, 8 Vet. App. 202 (1995); see also Mitchell v. Shinseki, 25 Vet. App. 32, 44 (2011). Nonetheless, even when the background factors listed in § 4.40 or 4.45 are relevant when evaluating a disability, the rating is assigned based on the extent to which motion is limited, pursuant to 38 C.F.R. § 4.71a; a separate or higher rating under § 4.40 or 4.45 itself [*27] is not appropriate. See Thompson v. McDonald, 815 F.3d 781, 785 (Fed. Cir. 2016). 

In Correia v. McDonald, 28 Vet. App. 158 (2016), the Court specified additional requirements that VA examiners should address when assessing musculoskeletal disabilities, holding specifically that the joints involved should be tested for pain on both active and passive motion, in weight-bearing and non-weight-bearing and, if possible, with the range of the opposite undamaged joint.

In addition, assignment of a disability rating should consider limitation of functional ability during flare-ups or when a joint is used repeatedly over a period of time. See DeLuca 8 Vet. App. 202. Specifically, in Sharp v. Shulkin, 29 Vet. App. 26 (2017), the Court stated that flare-ups must be considered in providing an estimate of additional functional loss based on range of motion.

Diagnostic Code 5003 and 38 C.F.R. § 4.59 indicate that painful motion of a major joint caused by degenerative arthritis is entitled to a minimum 10 percent rating per joint even if there is no actual limitation of motion. Lichtenfels v. Derwinski, 1 Vet. App. 484, 488 (1991). 

The Board notes that effective February 7, 2021, VA revised the criteria for evaluating musculoskeletal disorders. VA's General Counsel has held that where a law or regulation changes during the pendency of a claim for a higher rating, the Board must first determine whether the revised version is more favorable to the veteran. In so doing, it may be necessary for the Board to apply both the old and new versions of the regulation. If the revised version of the regulation is more favorable, the retroactive reach of that regulation under 38 U.S.C. § 5110(g) can be no earlier than the effective date of that change. The Board must generally apply both the former and the revised versions of the regulation for the period prior and subsequent to the regulatory change, but an effective date based on the revised criteria may be no earlier than the date of the change.

Impairment of the knee is specifically rated pursuant to 38 C.F.R. § 4.71a, Diagnostic Code 5256 to 5262. Normal range of motion of the knee is to zero degrees extension and to 140 degrees flexion. See 38 C.F.R. § 4.71a, Plate II.

Under Diagnostic Code 5257, a 10 percent rating will be assigned for recurrent subluxation or instability due to sprain, incomplete ligament tear, or complete ligament tear (repaired, unrepaired, or failed repair) causing persistent instability, without a prescription from a medical provider for an assistive device (e.g., cane(s), crutch(es), walker) or bracing for ambulation. A 20 percent rating will be assigned for instability with either sprain, incomplete ligament tear, or repaired complete ligament tear causing persistent instability, and a medical provider prescribes a brace and/or assistive device (e.g., cane(s), crutch(es), walker) for ambulation; or with unrepaired or failed repair of complete ligament tear causing persistent instability, and a medical provider prescribes either an assistive device (e.g., cane(s), crutch(es), walker) or bracing for ambulation. A 30 percent rating will be assigned for instability with unrepaired or failed repair of complete ligament tear causing persistent instability, and a medical provider prescribes both an assistive device (e.g., cane(s), crutch(es), walker) and bracing for ambulation. 

Under Diagnostic Code 5260, a noncompensable rating will be assigned for limitation of flexion of the leg to 60 degrees; a 10 percent rating will be assigned for limitation of flexion of the leg to 45 degrees; a 20 percent rating will be assigned for limitation of flexion of the leg to 30 degrees; and a 30 percent rating will be assigned for limitation of flexion of the leg to 15 degrees. See 38 C.F.R. § 4.71a. 

Under Diagnostic Code 5261, a noncompensable percent rating will be assigned for limitation of extension of the leg to 5 degrees; a 10 percent rating will be assigned for limitation of extension of the leg to 10 degrees; a 20 percent rating will be assigned for limitation of extension of the leg to 15 degrees; a 30 percent  rating will be assigned for limitation of extension of the leg to 20 degrees; a 40  percent rating will be assigned for limitation of extension of the leg to 30 degrees; and, a 50 percent rating will be assigned for limitation of extension of the leg to 45 degrees. Id.

While the revised criteria did not affect rating of the Veteran's knee strain, the Board notes that prior to February 7, 2021, VA would have rated knee instability as slight (10 percent), moderate (20 percent), or severe (30 percent). The Board finds the rating criteria prior to February 7, 2021, to be more favorable to rating the Veteran's left knee instability.  

The Appellant contends that the Veteran's left knee instability is entitled to a higher rating for the periods on appeal. The Veteran's left knee instability was characterized as slight and rated as 10 percent disabling effective May 3, 2011, the date he filed a claim regarding his knee. His left knee instability was characterized as moderate and rated as 20 percent disabling effective February 10, 2020.  

The Appellant also contends that the Veteran's left knee strain is entitled to a higher rating for the periods on appeal. The Veteran's left knee strain was rated as 10 percent disabling effective May 3, 2011, the date he filed a claim regarding his knee. The Veteran's left knee strain was later increased to 20 percent disabling effective April 29, 2018. The Veteran's 10 percent rating was based on painful motion because his knee manifested in painful but noncompensable limitation of flexion and extension. 38 C.F.R. §§ 4.59, 4.71a. The Veteran's 20 percent rating was based on limitation of extension to 15 degrees. 

The Veteran's medical records indicate that in April 2011, the Veteran reported constant, daily knee pain occurring for the prior two weeks. The pain was reported as not going away with rest, ice, or other measures and that the Veteran could barely walk on it. See Medical Treatment Record - Non-Governmental Facility of June 16, 2011.

In a March 2012 VA examination, the Veteran reported his knee caused him difficulty with walking and he had constant use of a cane. 

In March 2012, the Veteran's private treatment records document that the Veteran reported pain in his left knee without popping, locking, or grinding. He reported his knee would buckle and he had walked with a cane for approximately two years. The Veteran reported his knee would swell to the point where he can barely walk on it. He also reported his knee felt unstable to a moderate degree; one of the medical recommendations was to decrease the risk of falling due to his knee giving way. See Medical Treatment Record - Non-Governmental Facility of September 24, 2012.

In April 2018, the Veteran was afforded an additional VA exam. The examiner noted the Veteran reported knee pain when walking long distances or standing too long. He also reported flare-ups of more severe pain with weather changes, and he regularly used a cane. The Veteran had limited range of motion with pain. Based on this exam, the Veteran's rating for left knee strain was increased from 10 to 20 percent due to limitation of extension. 

In February 2020, the Veteran was afforded an additional VA exam. The examiner noted the Veteran was now using a walker and he was unable to stand for longer than a few minutes and only with the walker.

The April 2018 and February 2020 VA exams were both found to be inadequate per Correia, cited above, due to the examiner's failing to test for pain on both active and passive motion, in weight-bearing and non-weight-bearing and, if possible, with the range of the opposite undamaged joint.

In March, April, and October 2022, January, March, April, July, and October 2023, additional VA examinations and medical opinions were obtained. However, by this time the Veteran was deceased so no in-person examination could be performed, and the examiners had to rely on the evidence of record in rendering their opinions. These opinions were found to be inadequate either by relying on transposed data or failing to consider lay evidence and private medical evidence in providing a retrospective opinion on the functional impacts of the Veteran's left knee disabilities. 

As noted above, in July 2024, the Board again remanded these matters. 

In August 2024, the examiner opined that the Veteran's knee mildly worsened between the 2018 and 2020 VA exams and specified that the "+1" notation in April 2018 indicated moderate instability. The examiner conceded that swelling and other factors would have impacted the Veteran's range of motion had the proper tests been conducted; however, the examiner was unable to provide range of motion estimates without speculation. 

In October 2024, the examiner provided additional amplification and clarification. He again opined that range of motion estimates would be pure speculation as symptoms can wax and wane from day to day or even throughout the day. He also opined that the Veteran's left knee instability started as mild and became moderate as shown by February 2020 use of a walker; however, this opinion is not consistent with the examiner's August 2024 assertion that the Veteran's instability was moderate as of April 2018.

The Board finds that the Veteran's consistent reporting of his left knee instability most closely presented as moderate from May 3, 2011, and as severe from February 10, 2020. As documented in the March 2012 VA exam, the Veteran was already reliant on a cane for ambulation; the record is not clear whether the cane was medically prescribed. In February 2020, the Veteran's knee instability was documented as having worsened and the Veteran graduated from a cane to use of a walker. Resolving any reasonable doubt in favor of the Veteran, an increased rating of 20 percent from May 3, 2011, to February 9, 2020, and of 30 percent from February 10, 2020, until the Veteran's death on April [Redacted], 2021, for left knee instability is therefore granted.

Unfortunately, despite numerous remands and medical opinions, the Board is unable to determine whether and to what extent the Veteran's range of motion in his left knee would have decreased had the proper testing been conducted. Accordingly, an increased rating for left knee strain for the period on appeal is denied. The Veteran consistently asserted his complaints of knee pain and knee instability and the Board finds that granting an increased rating for the Veteran's left knee instability best compensates him for the functional loss due to these multiple knee disabilities.

TDIU

The Board notes that the Veteran was granted TDIU based upon service-connected disabilities from January 22, 2019, to April [Redacted], 2021, in a February 2022 Board decision. 

The current appeal is for TDIU prior to January 22, 2019. In addition to the left knee strain and left knee instability discussed above, prior to January 22, 2019, the Veteran was also service connected for conversion reaction with a 10 percent rating effective July 22, 1951. The Veteran's combined rating was 30 percent effective May 3, 2011, and 40 percent effective April 30, 2018.  

A TDIU may be assigned, where the schedular rating is less than total, where a veteran is unable to secure or follow a substantially gainful occupation as a result of service-connected disabilities. 38 C.F.R. § 4.16(a). To qualify for schedular consideration of a TDIU, if there is only one such disability, this disability shall be ratable at 60 percent or more, and, if there are two or more disabilities, there shall be at least one disability ratable at 40 percent or more and sufficient additional disability to bring the combined rating to 70 percent or more. Id. 

Even with the increased rating for left knee instability granted above, the Veteran did not meet the schedular criteria for TDIU. In February 2022, the Board remanded this matter for extraschedular consideration. The Veteran's claim was referred to the Director of Compensation Service for extraschedular consideration. The Director considered whether a TDIU pursuant to 38 C.F.R. § 4.16(b) was warranted. In April 2022, the Director found that a TDIU was not warranted pursuant to 38 C.F.R. § 4.16(b) during the relevant rating period on appeal, noting that there was no evidence of the Veteran's inability to perform sedentary employment prior to January 22, 2019. See VA Memo of April 25, 2022, and VA Memo of April 27, 2022. 

The Veteran's work history shows that he worked in civil service until 1974 when he retired. See April 2019 VA treatment record. His death certificate notes that he had an 8th grade education. In June 1979, the Veteran reported working as a civil service worked for the Department of the Army from 1957 until his retirement in 1974. The Veteran subsequently worked part time as a machine operator and maintenance worker until 1978. See Medical Treatment Record - Governmental Facility of May 23, 1979. 

The Board is not bound by the Director's decision so it will exercise its de novo review authority to decide whether a TDIU is warranted in this case for the rating period on appeal. See Wages v. McDonald, 27 Vet. App. 233 (2015) (holding that a decision of TDIU under 38 C.F.R. § 4.16(b) by the Director of C&P is not evidence, and is not a policy decision, but is simply a decision or adjudication that is adopted by the RO and reviewed de novo by the Board). 

The persuasive weight of the evidence is against finding that the Veteran was unable to obtain or maintain substantially gainful employment as a result of his service-connected disabilities during the period on appeal. After a review of the evidence of record, while the Board finds the Veteran's service-connected disabilities may have some impact on his ability to fully function occupationally, the medical evidence does not show that his service-connected disabilities were so severe prior to January 22, 2019, that they prevented the Veteran from obtaining and sustaining gainful employment. 

The phrase "unable to secure and follow a substantially gainful occupation" contains both economic and noneconomic components. See Ray v. Wilkie, 31 Vet. App. 58, 73 (2019). The economic component refers to an occupation earning more than marginal income (outside of a protected environment) as determined by the U.S. Department of Commerce as the poverty threshold for one person. Id. The noneconomic component requires a determination as to a veteran's ability to secure and follow such employment. Id. Attention should be given to the veteran's history, education, skills, and training; whether the veteran has the physical ability (both exertional and nonexertional) to perform the types of activities required by the occupation at issue (e.g., lifting, bending, sitting, standing, walking, climbing, as well as auditory and visual limitations); and whether the veteran has the mental ability to perform the activities required by the occupation at issue (e.g., memory, concentration, ability to adapt to change, handle work place stress, get along with coworkers, and demonstrate reliability and productivity). Id. 

In a January 2019 decision, the Board remanded this matter for proper notice to the Veteran. The VA subsequently attempted to obtain a VA Form 21-8940 from the Veteran; however, no completed form was received. 

The August 2024 VA exam described above provided a medical opinion as to the functional impact of the Veteran's left knee disabilities. The examiner noted the Veteran has decreased tolerance to prolonged sitting, standing, and walking; repetitive squatting motions like going up/down the stairs also is limited.

Based on the foregoing, entitlement to a TDIU prior to January 22, 2019 is denied. In reaching the above conclusions the Board has considered the applicability of the benefit of the doubt doctrine. However, as there is not an approximate balance of positive and negative evidence regarding the claim that doctrine is not applicable in this case. See 38 U.S.C. § 5107(b); 38 C.F.R. § 3.102; Lynch v. McDonough, 21 F.4th 776 (Fed. Cir. 2021) (en banc). 

 

 

Ann K. Minami

Veterans Law Judge

Board of Veterans' Appeals

Attorney for the Board	H.D. Partridge

The Board's decision in this case is binding only with respect to the instant matter decided. This decision is not precedential and does not establish VA policies or interpretations of general applicability. 38 C.F.R. § 20.1303.
